raw_case_text: A 10-day-old male presented with high-grade fever and jaundice for six days and seizures for two days. On examination, the baby was febrile, irritable, icteric, and hepatomegaly without eschar, rash, or petechiae. The abdomen was distended. The axillary temperature was 39.3  C, the pulse rate was 176/min, and the respiration rate was 46/min. A complete blood count showed that the white blood cells (WBCs) count was 24.76x109/L with 76.4% lymphocytes, 12.1% neutrophils, and 8.1% monocytes. Tests showed that the total bilirubin level was 87.4 micromol/L, aspartate aminotransferase level was 336.6 U/L, alanine aminotransferase level was 1317.1 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase level was 1477.6 U/L. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed a WBC count at 283x106/L with 95.1% mononuclear cells, 4.9% polymorphonuclear neutrophils, a protein concentration of 3.084 g/L and a glucose concentration of 1.18 mmol/L. Computed tomography (CT) showed patchy low-density areas in the bilateral frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes (Figure 1A). Tests for malaria, dengue, toxoplasmosis, leptospirosis, mycobacterium tuberculosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus were negative. A diagnosis of neonatal bacterial meningitis was made, and the patient was started on cefotaxime sodium combined with ampicillin and phenobarbital to control fever and seizures. On the third day of admission, his seizures and jaundice had subsided, but the fever persisted, and the CSF still showed abnormalities. We re-evaluated the family history and found that the patient's mother had anemia (Hb: 73 g/L) since the 28th week of pregnancy and reversed fever of unknown origin from three days before delivery to postpartum. On examination, there was an 1.2x0.8 cm eschar on her left groin (Figure 1B). The Weil-Felix test was positive for OXK 1:640 and 1:160 in the mother and baby, respectively, and both had positive IgM-ELISA 1:160 to the Karp antigen. Meanwhile, Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was positive for Orientia tsutsugamushi in both mother and baby (Supplementary Material). The final diagnosis of the baby was congenital infection of scrub typhus with bacterial meningitis. His treatment was immediately adjusted to intravenous azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day for three weeks and oral azithromycin for one week, and his mother was treated with oral tetracycline. After treatment, the baby and his mother's condition improved and stabilized. During the 4 weeks of hospitalization, the EEG, MRI, psychomotor assessment and Griffiths assessment were normal. No neurological sequelae were found after 6 months of follow-up. Written informed consent was obtained from the child's parents.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-day-old male neonate presented with a 6-day history of high-grade fever and jaundice and a 2-day history of seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born to a mother who experienced an undiagnosed febrile illness from 3 days pre-delivery into the postpartum period, the neonate developed high-grade fever and jaundice at 4 days of life and seizures at 8 days of life. Seizures and jaundice subsided by day 3 of empiric cefotaxime, ampicillin, and phenobarbital, but high fever and CSF pleocytosis persisted until maternal re-examination revealed a left inguinal eschar.
subjective.past_medical_history: Maternal history of third-trimester anemia (Hb 73 g/L from 28 weeks' gestation), peripartum fever of unknown origin starting 3 days before delivery, and a 1.2 x 0.8 cm left inguinal eschar.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for neonatal high-grade fever, irritability, jaundice, abdominal distension, and seizures.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (axillary temperature 39.3 C), irritable, icteric, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 46/min, distended abdomen, and hepatomegaly without cutaneous eschar, rash, or petechiae (mother had a 1.2 x 0.8 cm left groin eschar).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 24.76 x 10^9/L (76.4% lymphocytes, 12.1% neutrophils, 8.1% monocytes), total bilirubin 87.4 umol/L, AST 336.6 U/L, ALT 1,317.1 U/L, and LDH 1,477.6 U/L. Tests for malaria, toxoplasmosis, leptospirosis, M. tuberculosis, rubella, CMV, HSV, and JEV were negative. Weil-Felix OX-K titers were 1:640 in the mother and 1:160 in the neonate, and both mother and baby tested positive for Orientia tsutsugamushi Karp antigen IgM ELISA (1:160) and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Follow-up EEG was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: CSF examination revealed WBC 283 x 10^6/L (95.1% mononuclear cells, 4.9% polymorphs), markedly elevated protein of 3.084 g/L, and low glucose of 1.18 mmol/L. Head CT showed patchy low-density areas in the bilateral frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes; subsequent follow-up brain MRI was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Congenital scrub typhus (transplacental Orientia tsutsugamushi infection) complicated by meningoencephalitis/meningitis and severe neonatal hepatitis, confirmed by maternal left inguinal eschar, positive Weil-Felix OX-K (1:160 neonate, 1:640 mother), positive O. tsutsugamushi Karp IgM ELISA (1:160), and positive mNGS in both mother and infant. Dengue virus was ruled out by negative dengue testing. Switched from empiric cefotaxime/ampicillin to IV azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks) followed by 1 week of oral azithromycin (and maternal oral tetracycline), achieving complete clinical and developmental recovery without sequelae at 6-month follow-up.
